messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 54, Matiu Tanoa had spent most of his adult life in cockpits, and before the accident he had understood himself in simple, durable terms: disciplined, steady under pressure, the kind of combat pilot other people trusted when conditions turned complicated. He was a married Samoan American man who had built his life around precision and control. The accident happened during what should have been a manageable flight. In the air, something went badly wrong quickly enough that his training narrowed to survival. He remembered the violent change in the aircraft, the sensation that the space around him had become hostile, and the terrible arithmetic of seconds in which he had to judge whether he could still bring the aircraft down or whether he would have to get out. In those moments, his attention locked onto exits, trajectories, and the problem of how not to die. The idea of escape was not abstract; it was the difference between living and being trapped in a failing machine.

He survived, but the sense of danger did not stay in the past. In the weeks afterward, he found that he could not enter a room, restaurant, briefing space, or waiting area and settle until he had located a way out. He did this automatically at first, scanning doors, windows, side corridors, anything that might serve if something went wrong. He described it less as a choice than as a requirement before his body would let him sit down. If he and his wife met friends for dinner, he angled himself toward the entrance or the nearest clear exit and tracked how crowded the room was. If a hotel ballroom filled for an event, he noticed the fire doors before he heard a word anyone said. Even at home, where he would once have relaxed most easily, he remained watchful. He checked sight lines, listened for changes in sound, and was aware of entry points in a way that made his own house feel less like a refuge than a place he needed to secure.

His work environment sharpened this further. On base, where vigilance had always been valued, he could feel how different his attention had become from ordinary professional awareness. Walking through hangars or entering operations buildings, he was not simply observant; he was superalert, continuously tracking movement, exits, and anything unusual in the environment. In enclosed rooms he felt the old urgency from the aircraft return in quieter form, as though comfort depended on proving to himself that he could get out. Colleagues may have seen a seasoned pilot with strong situational awareness, but Matiu knew the experience from the inside as something harsher and more exhausting. He could not just arrive somewhere; he had to map it.

Over time, what troubled him most was not only the watchfulness but what he felt had happened to him as a person. He had come to believe that the accident had altered him in some permanent way. He said he had changed for the worse, and he did not say this dramatically. He meant it as a conclusion he had reached after months of recognizing himself less and less. The man who used to take pleasure in ordinary family life, in jokes at dinner, in the quiet satisfaction of routine, now often felt emotionally blunted. He looked at his wife and knew he loved her, yet he was frightened by how often his feelings seemed distant, muted, or inaccessible. He had begun to think, with a kind of resignation, that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again. That belief carried particular weight because emotional steadiness had once been part of how he understood his own character. Now he felt estranged from himself, as if the accident had split his life into a before and after and left him unsure which version of him remained.

That sense of identity loss extended beyond home. As a combat pilot, he had always relied on a coherent self-image: capable, focused, reliable. After the accident, he still moved through the routines of military life, but privately he felt unrecognizable. He was certain something essential had been damaged. He did not speak about this easily, partly because the language available to him sounded too vague for how concrete the loss felt. “I don’t know myself anymore” was the closest he could come. The statement held grief as much as fear.

By the time he sought help, the strain had become difficult to contain within the life he and his wife had built. She could see that even at home he was on guard, and he could see the cost of being physically present but emotionally harder to reach. He came to treatment not because he lacked discipline, but because discipline had not restored the man he believed he had been. What frightened him most was the possibility that this was final—that the hyperalertness, the constant search for exits, the emotional deadening, and the sense of being permanently changed were now simply his life. What he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was not to erase the accident but to find some way of living in which his home felt like home again and his own inner life no longer seemed closed off to him.
